### Holding up under impairment

Reconciliation disagreement is zero whenever the server saw every input;
it becomes non-zero only when inputs are lost or arrive too late to use.

### What TCP costs

Observed one-way delivery latency. The reliable column is the transport this
project actually ships on: a lost packet is retransmitted rather than dropped,
and everything behind it waits — head-of-line blocking.

| Loss | datagram p50 | datagram p99 | TCP-like p50 | **TCP-like p99** | retransmits |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1% loss | 51 ms | 70 ms | 49 ms | **181 ms** | 9 |
| 5% loss | 51 ms | 70 ms | 54 ms | **189 ms** | 44 |
| 10% loss | 51 ms | 70 ms | 59 ms | **445 ms** | 112 |

### Lag compensation

Inputs carry the tick the client simulated them at, and the server applies
each one there — rewinding and replaying when it arrives after that tick has
already been simulated. Without it a strike that plainly connected on the
player’s screen lands in the right place at the wrong moment, and misses.

Note what the correction columns do *not* say. Rewinding does not reduce
reconciliation corrections — it slightly increases them, because revising the
server’s past means a client that already reconciled against the pre-revision
snapshot has to be nudged again. The benefit is not fewer corrections; it is
that the input lands at the tick it was meant for, so the strike connects.
That property is asserted directly in `packages/server/test/rewind.test.ts`,
which checks a late input produces the same state as one that was never late.

| RTT (+30ms jitter) | late inputs/s | rewinds/s | avg rewind depth | correction p99, rewind **on** | correction p99, rewind **off** |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 ms | 0.4 | 1.0 | 1.0 | **0.0** | 0.0 |
| 150 ms | 3.3 | 4.8 | 1.2 | **0.0** | 0.0 |
| 300 ms | 12.8 | 11.7 | 2.3 | **2.2** | 34.2 |

| RTT | lead p50 | starved reports/s | discarded (beyond window)/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|

### Wire format

Three separate savings: no field names, 16-bit fixed-point instead of
`float64`, and a bitmask naming only the field groups that changed since the
previous snapshot. Delta encoding needs no keyframe recovery protocol here
because the transport is TCP — the same reliability that causes head-of-line
blocking guarantees no snapshot is ever missing.

| Conditions | JSON down | **binary down** | JSON up | **binary up** | reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| clean 100ms | 7.80 KiB/s | **0.95 KiB/s** | 5.56 KiB/s | **0.63 KiB/s** | 88% |
| 200ms + 50ms jitter | 7.90 KiB/s | **0.99 KiB/s** | 5.62 KiB/s | **0.63 KiB/s** | 88% |

What it costs: quantisation gives up bit-exact state reconstruction. A client
adopting a JSON snapshot resumes from the server’s exact numbers; one adopting
a quantised snapshot resumes from rounded ones, so replay can no longer be
bit-identical. The rounding step is ~0.018 units against a 0.05 correction
dead zone, and reconciliation re-syncs every 3 ticks, so it does not surface —
but it is a real property traded away rather than a free win.

| Conditions | codec | correction p50 | correction p99 | corrections/s |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| clean 100ms | JSON | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00 |
| clean 100ms | binary | 0.0 | 0.0 | 0.00 |
| 200ms + 50ms jitter | JSON | 0.1 | 3.4 | 0.13 |
| 200ms + 50ms jitter | binary | 0.1 | 4.3 | 0.38 |

### Puck strategies, head to head

How wrong the displayed puck was about the moment it claimed to depict,
in rink units. Recorded when the client draws tick T, resolved once the
server reaches T. The puck is 18 units across.

**A** is never wrong about the past — it shows real snapshot data. It is
wrong about *now*, which is what the player is looking at. **B** is right
about now until the opponent plays the puck, because their input has not
arrived; the failure lands in the tail. **C** predicts only while this
client owns the puck, taking B’s median and A’s tail.

`jump/s` counts frames where the displayed puck moved further than it
physically could — a visible teleport rather than motion. Accuracy alone
cannot see this, and it is half of what "feels right" means: a puck that is
consistently late still moves smoothly, while one that is usually exact but
occasionally snaps sideways reads as broken.

| RTT | A p50 | A p99 | A jump/s | B p50 | B p99 | B jump/s | **C p50** | **C p99** | **C jump/s** |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 ms | 0.0 | 214.1 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 93.7 | 0.1 | **0.0** | **173.2** | **0.1** |
| 100 ms | 168.8 | 280.1 | 0.1 | 0.0 | 219.8 | 0.6 | **24.4** | **234.4** | **0.4** |
| 200 ms | 162.6 | 394.0 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 192.3 | 0.8 | **0.2** | **327.4** | **0.6** |
| 300 ms | 183.5 | 580.5 | 0.1 | 0.0 | 473.5 | 0.6 | **55.0** | **381.0** | **0.4** |

No strategy wins outright, which is the honest result. B is the most
accurate and the least smooth; A is the smoothest and the least accurate;
C sits between them on both. What C actually buys is *where* its accuracy
goes:

The aggregate understates C, because it averages over frames where the puck
is at the far end and the player is watching rather than playing. Split by
who held authority, C is doing exactly what it was built to do — B’s
accuracy when you are about to hit the puck, A’s correctness when you are not:

| RTT | C, while you own it (p50 / p99) | C, while you do not (p50 / p99) | owned | handoffs/s |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 50 ms | **0.2 / 233.0** | 0.0 / 95.0 | 13% | 0.3 |
| 100 ms | **0.6 / 222.6** | 150.2 / 348.6 | 35% | 0.6 |
| 200 ms | **0.0 / 255.0** | 170.0 / 345.4 | 66% | 0.4 |
| 300 ms | **0.1 / 238.1** | 210.4 / 396.8 | 40% | 0.5 |

### How stale the puck looks (strategy A)

How far into the past the on-screen puck actually is, found by matching it
against recorded authoritative positions. Expected value is the
interpolation delay plus half the round trip — which is exactly the cost of
never predicting the puck, and what strategies B and C will reduce. The
delay is adaptive and settles near its floor on these links, so the
expected column uses that floor rather than the fixed value it replaced.

| RTT | expected | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 ms | ~58 ms | 67 ms | 67 ms | 167 ms |
| 50 ms | ~83 ms | 83 ms | 400 ms | 567 ms |
| 100 ms | ~108 ms | 117 ms | 117 ms | 133 ms |
| 200 ms | ~158 ms | 167 ms | 167 ms | 183 ms |
| 300 ms | ~208 ms | 217 ms | 217 ms | 217 ms |
